sketches.title: Paper Trail
sketches.premise: You and your opponent build a case one document at a time. Each turn, submit a standing piece of paperwork that overturns the document before it; the council decides whether your filing truly defeats the record. The clerk is watching, and yes, they look disappointed already.
sketches.criterion: A filing overcomes the standing document when it directly cancels, invalidates, replaces, exposes, or makes that document impossible to rely on; merely ignoring it, outlasting it, or submitting a larger version of the same claim loses.
sketches.move_shape: Name one document and its action in a sentence: "I am a signed withdrawal; I cancel the complaint." A bigger copy, a cousin from the same paperwork family, and a figure of speech without a real paper mechanism do not count—the clerk will not be impressed by your dramatic font.
sketches.first_card: A complaint: "I am a complaint, formally accusing the matter before the council."

sketches.title: Council Chain
sketches.premise: The council must pass one decision from member to member, but each speaker adds a standing rule that defeats the last rule. Build a chain of plain civic powers: a vote can reject a motion, an audit can expose a lie, and an emergency order can interrupt a meeting. The chair may bang the gavel, but cannot rescue a flimsy idea.
sketches.criterion: A new council act overcomes the standing act when it uses a different, understandable civic power to block, reverse, expose, replace, or legally outrank what stands; dodging, merely surviving, and saying the same act is bigger lose.
sketches.move_shape: State your council role or act and what it does: "I am an audit; I reveal the hidden numbers behind the budget." A bigger vote, a neighboring committee with the same trick, or "the council is a storm" as mere poetry earns a polite note in the minutes—and a sharper one from the host.
sketches.first_card: A motion: "I am a motion, asking the council to adopt one clear action."

sketches.title: Stamp Standoff
sketches.premise: Two office workers duel with official stamps. Each turn, choose one standing stamp or seal that defeats the mark before it: an approval can be voided, a date can expire a permit, and a court seal can force a decision. The winner is the worker whose ink makes the previous ink meaningless.
sketches.criterion: A mark overcomes the previous mark when its official function directly invalidates, limits, replaces, or ends the authority of that mark; avoiding the stamped paper, waiting it out, and using a larger or nearly identical stamp do not count.
sketches.move_shape: Name the standing mark and its effect: "I am a cancellation stamp; I cross out the approval." A bigger approval is still approval, a related seal is not automatically a counter, and calling your stamp a "dragon" without explaining what it does is just office-supply theater.
sketches.first_card: An approval stamp: "I am an approval stamp; I make this request officially allowed."

sketches.title: Permit Panic
sketches.premise: You are rival permit officers handling one growing pile of requests. On each turn, issue a standing permit, restriction, notice, or inspection that defeats what the other officer just issued. The council judge checks whether your paper rule actually controls the last one, rather than merely standing nearby looking official.
sketches.criterion: A civic notice overcomes the standing notice when it directly forbids, revokes, expires, exposes, or supersedes its permission or restriction; hiding from it, enduring it, or issuing a stronger-looking copy of the same kind loses.
sketches.move_shape: Give one official item and its practical effect: "I am a fire ban; I forbid the campfire permit from being used." A bigger permit is no solution, a related safety rule needs a distinct mechanism, and a metaphor like "I am the law's thunder" must explain the actual order or be filed under Fancy Nonsense.
sketches.first_card: A building permit: "I am a building permit; I allow one named construction job to begin."

sketches.title: Minutes to Midnight
sketches.premise: The council meeting is running late, and every turn adds one standing item to its official minutes. Your item must defeat the previous item by changing what the meeting can decide, hear, or do next. Win by making the record move forward, not by hiding behind the clock like a very nervous intern.
sketches.criterion: A meeting item overcomes the standing item when it directly closes, postpones, reopens, replaces, or makes the previous item inadmissible through a clear meeting procedure; mere delay, endurance, avoidance, and amplified repetition lose.
sketches.move_shape: Name the agenda item and its procedural action: "I am a motion to table; I postpone the debate before the vote." A longer delay is still delay, a related motion must have a different effect, and "the meeting is a black hole" is not a mechanism unless it actually closes the agenda.
sketches.first_card: A public comment: "I am a public comment; I place one spoken concern before the council."

sketches.title: Filing Cabinet Feud
sketches.premise: Two rival clerks control a cabinet of records. Each turn, place one standing record-handling action that defeats the previous one: a correction can fix an error, a subpoena can compel a file, and a destruction order can end its official life. The council judges the paperwork; the host judges your filing technique with considerably less mercy.
sketches.criterion: A record action overcomes the standing action when it directly corrects, compels, seals, replaces, or legally removes the result of that action; merely hiding, waiting, surviving, or using more of the same action does not count.
sketches.move_shape: Name the record action and its effect: "I am a correction notice; I replace the false address in the file with the true one." A bigger correction is still a correction, a nearby filing trick needs its own mechanism, and "I am an avalanche of papers" fails unless the avalanche actually does something to the record.
sketches.first_card: A filed report: "I am a filed report; I place a claim into the council's official record."
